diagnosis.balance: The balance grid was lying, and I have been reading it for five passes. state.mjs computed last-touched by stripping non-digits, so pre-loop work recorded as pre28/pre29/pre31 read as iterations 28/29/31 — it reported Courtyard as last=28 and River as last=31 in a run whose last iteration is 25. Fixed, and the real picture is different from the one I have been planning against: Courtyard & garden is 11 back (#14) and by far the most starved — the domain the piece is NAMED for and the thing SKILL.md calls the thing this piece is for. Then People & animals 6 back (#19), Lane & market 7 back (#18). Street 0 back, Plaza 1, River 2, Sky 3. This batch gives the courtyard the observer work in b26, the lane its first since #18 in b28, and life its first since #19 in b29. Sky takes two, but both are observer-side rather than more weather.

rationale:
Rung 5 — change the observer. Pass #20 said that if b20-b24 landed the next pass would climb, and all five landed and shipped.

The case for climbing is one number. The year is 26 sim days, which is ~24 real minutes at 1x. Nine systems now read season(): day length, light, the courtyard beds, all thirteen trees, the working day, the population caps, the weather fronts, the river, and as of #25 the allotment ceiling. Fourteen iterations, #12 through #25, went into making this town know what time of year it is. A person who opens the page and watches for thirty seconds sees two percent of that, and the sill under the canvas — which has said "Day 12 · Afternoon" since before the loop began — names the day and the hour and has never once named the season. The town is rich and only one view of it exists. That is the definition of rung 5, and it is also the answer to "what would most help somebody looking at this for thirty seconds": not another system, a way to reach the ones that are already there.

b25 and b27 are that argument in two sizes. b25 is the cheap half — say what season it is, in the sill, in the diorama own register. It is low risk and it is first because b27 needs a viewer who can already read the year before giving them a way to move through it. b27 is the batch bet and it is genuinely hard: every slow scalar in this town is rate-capped so that "it never steps" is a measurable guarantee, and the trees, beds, weather and river all carry hysteresis, so a jump to another season either respects the caps and takes real time or it is a pop. I have written it so that an honest transition counts as success and a teleport does not. It may fail; that is the one in this queue that could.

b26 is the other half of rung 5 and it goes to the starved domain. The diorama answers a click on 64% of the frame after #24, and the cursor says you may click here, but nothing says WHAT. There are eleven species in the beds with bloom stages, thirteen trees each on their own seasonal clock, and a viewer cannot name one of them. Naming what is under the pointer is a way to READ the town, which is the rung, and the courtyard is where the nameable content is densest — which is convenient, because the balance grid I just repaired says the courtyard has had nothing for eleven iterations. It is the domain the piece is named for.

b28 and b29 are not observer work and are in the queue deliberately, because five briefs on one theme is how a batch becomes a monoculture. b28 is the last flat system in the town: the market is three stalls every fourth day, identical in February and August, while fifty feet away the allotments ripen, are picked, rest and re-sow on a full year and gardeners walk out carrying baskets that go nowhere. It is the best remaining "these two systems should know about each other" and it lands in a domain 7 back. b29 closes c11, open since #5, which was blocked on a seam — routeToExit() — that now exists; street sitters get up when the sky thickens and courtyard sitters sit through the rain.

Curation, which was half this pass. The budget was 55.0 KB against a 46 KB cap and is now 45.3. Three things had to be true at once. LAWS.md had eleven promotions waiting from #21-#25 and was already at 11.0/12 KB, so eight of the eleven went in as MERGES into laws that already existed — presence-vs-rate into the time-compression law, the ten-seed rule into the R()-reshuffle law, the neutrality algebra into the slow-scalar law, footprint-off-the-grid into one-predicate-one-definition, the census ladder into pin-the-instant, grain-matching into the ceiling law. Only three are new and all three are about slow things: hysteresis across a phase boundary (#21, and #23 independently re-derived it through a long-lived object rather than a scalar, which is the loop generalising rather than repeating), duration-is-not-the-inverse-of-rarity, and they sit together. To pay for them I cut the flat-peak law into the slow-scalar law where it belonged, folded read-probes-first into the probe-rewind law, merged the two rate-of-zero laws, and compressed the register throughout — the essayistic style was itself the cost. 27 laws to 25, sharper, and inside the byte cap.

The ledger: the last three entries were 5.7, 4.3 and 4.9 KB against a cap I set at 3.5 KB last pass and did not enforce. Full text of all three appended to LEDGER-archive.md, condensed in place to 2.9/2.8/3.0, cap tightened to 3.0 KB, and — the actual fix — rotate-ledger.mjs now measures the last three entries by name and refuses to be quiet about one that is over. I run that script every pass, so it is no longer possible for me to miss this the way I missed it twice.

And a bug worth recording. state.mjs computed each domain last-touched iteration by stripping non-digits from the coverage entries, so pre-loop work tagged pre28, pre29, pre31 parsed as iterations 28, 29 and 31 — in a run that has reached 25. The grid told me Courtyard was the freshest domain when it is the most starved by seven iterations, and I have planned three passes against it. Balance is one of the two things I exist for and my instrument for it was inverted. Fixed, and it now prints how many iterations back each domain is.

queue.brief: The market is the last flat system in the town: three stalls, every fourth day, identical in February and August. Fifty feet away the allotments now ripen, are picked, rest and re-sow across a full year, gardeners arrive at a rate that reads ripePlots(), and they walk out carrying a basket (a.crop) that goes nowhere. Connect them — what the stalls carry should follow what the plots have actually produced, so a February market is thin and root-heavy and an August one is full. Why now: it is the best remaining "these two systems should know about each other" in the town, and the lane has had nothing since #18.
queue.successLooksLike: Two market mornings pinned six months apart are visibly different stalls, and a probe can name which plots the difference came from.
queue.avoid: Do not add a fourth stall type — three exist and the census says they are under-used. Do not give the market its own arrival source; it already has a spawn band under laneCap, and the whole east half competes for that one budget. Watch the autumn shoulder: bloomCap is stepped 3/2/1 while everything around it lerps (c50), so a market driven off ripeness will inherit that cliff.

queue.brief: Street sitters get up when the sky thickens — they refuse a seat above weatherComing() 0.42 and are released over 0.55..0.88 off a per-agent a.wary. Courtyard sitters, the picnic pairs on the lawn and the people on the benches, sit through the rain, because the gate at the sit branch reads a.street. This is c11, open since #5, and the reason it stayed open was that a courtyard sit is assigned at a waypoint with no route left, so refusing it would despawn somebody mid-lawn. routeToExit(a) now exists. Close it.
queue.successLooksLike: A front building over the courtyard empties the lawn and the benches at the same staggered per-person rate the cafe tables already empty at, and nobody vanishes where they sat.
queue.avoid: Do not give courtyard sitters umbrellas by default — the ~30% who get caught out is a deliberate reading. A picnic pair arrives together and shares a blanket, so do not let one half leave without the other.
